name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
title: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
answer: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries covers legal questions about whether and how software systems that act with little or no human intervention can hold duties, own assets, or be held responsible. It includes debates over legal personhood for AI, the use of decentralized autonomous organizations as vehicles for automated decision making, and the imposition of fiduciary standards on AI agents that manage money, property, or personal data. The field sits at the boundary of corporate law, trust law, agency law, and technology regulation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries covers legal questions about whether and how software systems that act with little or no human intervention can hold duties, own assets, or be held responsible. It includes debates over legal personhood for AI, the use of decentralized autonomous organizations as vehicles for automated decision making, and the imposition of fiduciary standards on AI agents that manage money, property, or personal data. The field sits at the boundary of corporate law, trust law, agency law, and technology regulation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practical infrastructure for this area is a mix of corporate registries, smart contract platforms, model registries, and compliance tooling. An autonomous entity may be formed through a limited liability company or foundation that wraps a set of smart contracts, while an AI fiduciary typically operates through a licensed financial or legal service with model logging and audit trails. These systems rely on identity verification, transaction ledgers, and governance or kill switches that allow human overseers to intervene.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work in this field is done through doctrinal legal analysis, regulatory drafting, and empirical tracking of cases and bills. Lawyers and researchers compare existing fiduciary duties of care, loyalty, and prudence against the behavior of automated systems, and they test whether existing entity forms can accommodate code based governance. Model governance assessments and incident reviews are used to map how an AI system made a decision, which is essential for any claim about breach of duty.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who bears liability when an autonomous entity causes harm and who can enforce a fiduciary duty against a machine. Provenance matters because a court or regulator must be able to trace the data, model version, and human approvals behind a decision. The site's tracking of 142 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents provides a current view of how courts are testing these duties in areas such as intellectual property, consumer protection, and securities.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The likely direction is toward limited legal recognition for autonomous entities, such as registered AI agents with narrow capacity to contract, and toward explicit fiduciary rules for AI systems that manage other people's assets. State legislatures are already producing a large volume of AI bills, and some proposals would create registration or licensing schemes for high risk autonomous systems. Over time, courts and regulators may develop a tiered framework where simple automation gets agency treatment, while systems with discretionary power over money or welfare attract fiduciary duties.
